strengths: Addresses an important limitation of single-frame VLA policies: observations can be ambiguous without execution history, particularly for repeated actions and ordered manipulation.
The architecture coherently combines perceptual and semantic memory, temporal retrieval, gated fusion, and bounded memory consolidation with a diffusion action policy.

Evaluation spans multiple simulation benchmarks and two physical robot platforms. Reported gains are substantial against CogACT, especially on real-world temporal tasks: 83 versus 57 in average progress score.

Component ablations provide preliminary evidence supporting complementary memory streams, gated fusion, and consolidation. The appendix supplies useful task descriptions, scoring rules, and training settings.
weaknesses: The central attribution to memory is insufficiently controlled. There is no otherwise identical model with memory disabled while retaining the added perceptual pathway and modified action expert. Nor are matched frame-stacking or recurrent alternatives evaluated on the real-world temporal tasks. Consequently, improvements over CogACT cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed memory mechanism.

Ablations are restricted to four relatively short SimplerEnv-Bridge tasks, with only 24 trials per task. They do not establish which components matter on the long-horizon tasks motivating the paper, where memory capacity increases from 16 to 256. Several improvements correspond to only a few additional successful trials, and no training-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported.

Checkpoint selection and baseline comparability weaken the headline results. Simulation results use the best checkpoint across repeated benchmark evaluations without clearly identifying a separate held-out final test. LIBERO-Long and LIBERO-90 are trained jointly, but equivalent training access for comparison methods is not established. Table 3 also compares averages over different sets of suites.

The abstract's 84% real-world 'success rate' conflates binary task success with partial-progress scores. Temporal-task scoring awards credit for incomplete execution, slight button contact, and some counting errors. These scores are useful but do not establish an 83% full-task completion rate. Full completion rates and uncertainty are needed, particularly with only 10–15 temporal-task trials.

Important memory-training details remain unspecified: causal ordering and masking for randomly sampled LIBERO frames, memory persistence and resets across batches, gradient propagation through stored entries, and timestamp handling after consolidation. These omissions make it difficult to verify that training faithfully matches causal online inference or to reproduce the main mechanism.

The methodological advance is primarily a combination of established attention, gating, averaging, and diffusion components; the cognitive analogy does not itself establish novelty. Stronger controlled evidence is therefore essential. Efficiency claims also lack latency, memory-use, and throughput measurements, particularly for retrieval over 256 perceptual tokens per entry with a 256-entry bank.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful limitation of single-observation VLA policies: visually similar states can require different actions depending on execution history. Button sequencing and counting provide useful motivating examples.
The architecture coherently combines perceptual and language-conditioned representations with memory retrieval, gated fusion, and bounded memory consolidation.

Evaluation is broad, covering SimplerEnv, all five LIBERO suites, and 12 real-world tasks. Reported improvements over CogACT are substantial, particularly the 26-point increase in real-world temporal-task scores.

The appendix provides useful implementation settings, task descriptions, scoring rules, and additional robustness experiments. Component ablations support the potential value of using both memory streams.
weaknesses: The central contribution is not adequately isolated. Tables 5–6 lack a memory-free version retaining the same perceptual pathway and modified action expert, so improvements over CogACT cannot be attributed specifically to memory. There are also no controlled comparisons against frame stacking, recurrent state, or a simple history transformer on the real-world temporal tasks. Existing temporal methods appear in simulation tables, but these comparisons do not establish the advantage of the proposed memory design under matched conditions.

LIBERO comparisons have an unresolved training-data confound. MemoryVLA jointly trains on Long and LIBERO-90, whereas the paper does not establish that reproduced and published baselines receive the same joint training data. This particularly affects interpretation of the Long-suite improvement. Table 3 additionally mixes four-suite and five-suite averages, making its aggregate ranking less directly comparable.

Checkpoint selection and uncertainty reporting weaken the empirical evidence. Sections 4.2–4.3 report the best validation checkpoint across frequent evaluations without clearly specifying a separate final test evaluation. Bridge uses only 24 trials per task, and its ablation improvements of 2.1–5.2 points correspond to roughly two to five additional successes across 96 trials. No repeated-training results or confidence intervals establish the reliability of these differences.

The headline real-world '84.0% success rate' combines binary success rates for general tasks with partial-progress scores for temporal tasks. The latter permit credit for incomplete execution and, in some tasks, imperfect actions. Although Appendix C.3 explains the scoring, an 83% temporal score does not establish an 83% task-completion rate. Full-completion rates and uncertainty are needed, especially with only 10–15 temporal trials per task.

Essential memory-training details remain ambiguous. Appendix B.3 describes sequential batches and randomly sampled within-episode frames, but does not specify chronological ordering, causal memory access, gradient detachment or backpropagation through stored entries, and memory handling across batches and episode boundaries. These omissions prevent verification that training matches causal deployment. The timestep assigned to merged entries is also unspecified.

Novelty is primarily architectural integration: cross-attention retrieval, sigmoid gating, adjacent-token averaging, and diffusion control are established mechanisms. The cognitive-science analogy does not itself establish a new computational principle, and the experiments provide limited evidence that the proposed perceptual–cognitive division offers advantages beyond conventional feature-level temporal memory.

Efficiency and robustness claims lack sufficient comparative support. No latency, throughput, or memory measurements are reported, including for the 256-entry real-world temporal memory. Appendix A evaluates OOD performance without corresponding baseline or memory-ablation results, so robustness cannot be attributed to the proposed mechanism; some shifts also cause substantial degradation, such as Coke Can performance falling from 92% to 42% under camera changes.

strengths: Addresses an important limitation of single-observation VLA policies: visually similar states can require different actions depending on execution history.
The architecture is coherent and practically motivated, combining perceptual and semantic memories with temporal retrieval, gated fusion, and bounded-capacity consolidation.

Evaluation is unusually broad, covering SimplerEnv, all five LIBERO suites, and 12 real-world tasks. Reported improvements over CogACT include 14.6 percentage points on Bridge, 4.6 on Fractal, and 26 points in real-world temporal-task progress scores.

Component ablations provide initial support for combining both memory streams and using gated fusion and consolidation. The appendix supplies useful task descriptions, scoring rules, and training details.
weaknesses: The experiments do not adequately isolate the central contribution. There is no otherwise identical model with history disabled, nor a matched frame-stacking or recurrent-memory baseline. Because the method also introduces direct perceptual conditioning of the action expert, improvements over CogACT cannot be attributed cleanly to temporal memory.

LIBERO comparisons have a material training-data confound: MemoryVLA jointly trains on Long and LIBERO-90, whereas equivalent joint training is not established for the reported baselines. Table 3 also mixes averages over four and five suites, weakening aggregate comparisons.

Statistical evidence is limited. Bridge uses only 24 trials per task, real-world temporal tasks use 10–15 trials, and no confidence intervals or variation across training seeds are reported. Several ablation gains correspond to only a few additional successful trials. Reporting the best repeatedly evaluated checkpoint without clearly distinguishing validation from final held-out evaluation creates selection-bias concerns.

The abstract calls the real-world aggregate an 84% success rate, but temporal tasks use partial-progress scores, including credit for incorrect placements and imperfect button presses. These scores are useful but do not establish an 83% temporal-task completion rate; full-episode success should be reported separately.

All memory ablations are on four relatively short Bridge tasks, rather than the temporal tasks motivating the paper. The real-world temporal configuration uses memory length 256, but capacity ablations cover only 4, 16, and 64. Consequently, the claimed long-horizon benefits of retrieval and consolidation remain insufficiently tested.

Novelty is primarily architectural integration of established attention, gating, and similarity-merging mechanisms. The cognitive-science analogy does not itself establish distinct semantic and episodic functionality, and the paper provides little representation or retrieval analysis to substantiate that interpretation.

Important implementation and efficiency details remain unclear: causal ordering of randomly sampled LIBERO frames, gradient propagation through stored memories, timestamp updates after merging, and inference latency and memory use at capacity 256. These omissions limit reproducibility and support for efficiency claims.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful limitation of single-frame VLA policies: visually ambiguous states that require remembering earlier observations. The dual perceptual/cognitive memory architecture is coherent and integrates naturally with a diffusion action expert.

Evaluation is unusually broad, spanning SimplerEnv, five LIBERO suites, Mikasa-Robo, and 12 real-world tasks. Reported improvements include 41.2% versus 29.4% on Mikasa-Robo and an 83 versus 57 partial-progress score on real-world temporal tasks.

Includes relevant temporal baselines, notably a reproduced CronusVLA on Mikasa-Robo, alongside component ablations, retrieval visualizations, robustness experiments, and inference measurements. Appendix ablations extend fusion and consolidation comparisons beyond SimplerEnv.
The reported inference overhead is modest: 0.194 versus 0.187 seconds per action chunk on RTX 4090. Detailed task descriptions and real-world scoring rules improve interpretability.
weaknesses: The central attribution to memory remains insufficiently controlled. There is no otherwise identical model with memory disabled while retaining the added perceptual pathway and action architecture. Cognitive-only and perceptual-only memory ablations do not resolve this confound. Matched recurrent or frame-window alternatives on the same backbone, particularly on real-world temporal tasks, would better establish the contribution of the proposed design.

Evaluation comparability needs clarification. LIBERO-10 and LIBERO-90 are trained jointly, whereas the manuscript does not establish equivalent training-data access for the comparison methods. Simulation results use the best checkpoint over repeated validation, but an independent final test protocol is not specified. These choices complicate interpretation of relatively small benchmark gains.

Statistical evidence is limited: no training-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported, Bridge uses only 24 trials per task, and temporal real-world tasks use 10–15 trials. Some architectural ablation gains correspond to only a few additional successful episodes. Real-world temporal scores measure partial progress, so the headline 83% should not be interpreted as full-task completion.

Novelty is primarily an integration of established components: feature memory, cross-attention retrieval, gated fusion, and similarity-based merging. The cognitive-science analogy provides motivation but does not establish that the learned streams implement distinct cognitive functions or that consolidation preserves task-critical information.

There are substantive reporting inconsistencies. Tables 3 and 17 assign different LIBERO results to CronusVLA and 4D-VLA; the CronusVLA row in Table 17 matches the 4D-VLA row in Table 3. The claim of highest performance on every Mikasa-Robo task contradicts Table 4, where MemoryVLA trails alternatives on Intercept and RememberColor3.

Important implementation details remain unclear, including gradient propagation through stored memories, memory handling across training batches and episode boundaries, and timestamp updates after merging. Efficiency measurements do not specify the memory capacity, leaving the cost of the 256-entry real-world configuration uncertain. Robustness and zero-shot experiments lack comparative baselines, and the latter uses only five trials per task.

strengths: Addresses an important limitation of single-observation VLA policies: visually ambiguous situations requiring memory of earlier events. Combining perceptual and semantic history is a plausible, useful architectural contribution.

The evaluation is substantial, spanning SimplerEnv, LIBERO, Mikasa-Robo, and 12 real-world tasks across multiple embodiments. Particularly compelling reported results include 88% on ShellGameTouch and a 26-point improvement over CogACT in real-world temporal-task scores.
Includes relevant temporal baselines, including reproduced CronusVLA results on Mikasa-Robo and additional comparisons in Appendix J.

Ablations support using both memory streams, gated fusion, and consolidation. Additional long-horizon ablations, retrieval visualizations, and inference measurements strengthen the empirical analysis.
weaknesses: The central memory contribution is not cleanly isolated. There is no matched version retaining the same perceptual pathway, action expert, and training procedure while removing historical memory. Comparisons against CogACT therefore conflate memory with other architectural changes. Controlled recurrent or frame-history alternatives on the real-world temporal suite would also strengthen the evidence.

Checkpoint selection and statistical reliability remain unresolved. Results use the best validation checkpoint across many evaluations, but an independent final test protocol is not clearly specified. No training-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported. With only 24 trials per Bridge task, the 2.1-point positional-encoding gain represents approximately two additional successes across the suite.

Important comparison results are internally inconsistent. Table 3 assigns the LIBERO scores 93.8/92.8/95.6/86.5 to 4D-VLA, whereas Table 17 assigns them to CronusVLA and gives different 4D-VLA results. Section 4.4 also incorrectly claims the highest performance on every Mikasa task: MemoryVLA trails PI-0 on Intercept and OpenVLA-OFT on RememberColor3. These issues require correction before the comparative claims can be trusted.

Reproducibility of the recurrent computation is incomplete. Appendix C describes frame sampling but does not clearly specify sequential memory updates within batches, gradient detachment or backpropagation through memory, or memory handling across episode boundaries. The timestamp assigned to a merged entry is also unspecified, despite its importance to temporal retrieval.

Real-world temporal results measure partial-credit progress, not full-task completion. The scoring rules are disclosed, which is helpful, but completion rates should also be reported to establish reliable long-horizon execution. Most temporal tasks use only 10 trials, and no temporal-context competitor is evaluated on this suite.

Novelty is primarily architectural integration of established attention, gating, feature caching, and similarity-based merging. The cognitive analogy does not establish a distinct computational principle. Generalization evidence is also limited: additional OOD experiments lack baseline comparisons, and zero-shot transfer uses only five trials per variant of closely related pick-and-place tasks.

strengths: Addresses an important limitation of single-frame VLA policies: visually ambiguous states that require historical context. The dual perceptual/cognitive memory, gated retrieval, and bounded consolidation form a coherent, practically motivated architecture.

Broad evaluation provides concrete positive evidence across SimplerEnv, LIBERO, Mikasa-Robo, and 12 real-world tasks. Particularly compelling results include 88% on ShellGameTouch versus 47% for the strongest listed baseline, and an average real-world temporal-task score of 83 versus CogACT's 57.

Includes relevant temporal baselines, including reproduced CronusVLA results on Mikasa-Robo and additional comparisons in Appendix J. MemoryVLA also achieves strong LIBERO performance using only third-person RGB.

Ablations support complementary memory streams and the benefits of gating and consolidation, with additional experiments beyond Bridge in the appendix. Reported inference latency increases modestly from 0.187 to 0.194 seconds on RTX 4090.
weaknesses: The main causal claim is incompletely isolated. There is no otherwise identical no-memory model retaining the added perceptual pathway and modified action expert, nor a matched simple history-encoder baseline. Comparisons with CogACT therefore cannot cleanly attribute improvements to the proposed memory mechanism. The novelty is primarily an integration of established components.

Statistical reliability and checkpoint selection need clarification. Bridge uses only 24 trials per task and real-world temporal tasks use 10–15 trials, without confidence intervals or training-seed variability. Several ablation gains represent only a few successful episodes. Reporting the best validation checkpoint without clearly documenting separate final evaluation seeds leaves potential selection bias unresolved.

Real-world temporal results measure partial-credit progress, not full-task completion. The scoring rules are disclosed, but full-completion rates are needed to assess reliable long-horizon execution. These experiments also lack a temporal-context baseline, making the architectural advantage over simpler memory approaches uncertain.

There are material reporting inconsistencies. Tables 3 and 17 assign different LIBERO results to CronusVLA and 4D-VLA; the 92.2% row changes attribution. Section 4.4 incorrectly claims the highest performance on every Mikasa task, despite lower results on Intercept and RememberColor3. LIBERO averages also mix four-suite and five-suite evaluations.

Implementation details remain incomplete for the central recurrent mechanism: gradient propagation through stored entries, memory handling across batches and episode boundaries, and timestamp updates after consolidation are insufficiently specified. Joint training on LIBERO-10 and LIBERO-90 also requires confirmation that comparisons use equivalent training data.

Efficiency and generalization claims need narrower qualification. The efficiency table does not specify memory-bank occupancy or establish overhead at the 256-entry real-world setting; its 82.5 Hz figure counts predicted actions rather than fresh observation-conditioned decisions. OOD studies lack baseline comparisons, and zero-shot task generalization uses only five trials per task.
